\section{Background}

\subsection{Alignment and costs}

Let \(A=a_1\dots a_n\) be the reference and \(B=b_1\dots b_m\) the query, and let cell \((i,j)\) lie on diagonal \(j-i\). Under gap-affine costs \((x, o, e)\), for example (4, 6, 2), a match costs 0, a mismatch \(x\) and a gap of \(k\) letters \(g(k)=o+ke\); unit costs have \(x=e=1\) and \(o=0\), two-piece costs take the minimum of two such functions \citep{Li2018minimap2}, and a substitution matrix instead scores each pair of letters. Global alignment compares two whole sequences; ends-free alignment places a read inside a longer window or finds the overlap of two reads; extension grows an alignment from a seed match \citep{Li2018minimap2}; and local alignment finds the best-matching parts of two sequences. Extension, local and, where asked, ends-free alignment instead maximise a score that rewards matches (Section 3.8). An alignment is \emph{optimal} if no alignment has a lower cost, or a higher score, under the requested costs and mode; a caller may further restrict alignments to a band of diagonals or a maximum cost, and an exact aligner then returns an optimal alignment among those or reports that none exists. At unit costs the distance \(D(i,j)\) between the prefixes \(a_1\dots a_i\) and \(b_1\dots b_j\) satisfies

\begin{equation}\begin{gathered}
D(i,j) = \min\bigl(D(i-1,j)+1,\; D(i,j-1)+1,\\ D(i-1,j-1)+[a_i \ne b_j]\bigr),
\end{gathered}\end{equation}

where \([a_i \ne b_j]\) is 1 if the letters differ and 0 otherwise, with \(D(i,0)=i\) and \(D(0,j)=j\), and the distance is \(D(n,m)\); gap-affine costs need three such layers \citep{Gotoh1982}.

\subsection{Band doubling and bit-parallel computation}

At unit costs, an alignment of cost at most \(t\) visits only diagonals \(d\) with \(|d| + |d - \delta| \le t\), where \(\delta = m - n\); band doubling computes only those cells, doubling \(t\) until \(D(n,m) \le t\) \citep{Ukkonen1985}. Myers' recurrence advances the score differences of 64 cells of a column, held in two machine words, by one column at a time \citep{Myers1999bitvector}, and A*PA2 computes the band in tiles of 256 columns with SIMD vectors \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa2}.

\subsection{Diagonal transition}

Diagonal transition keeps, for each cost \(s\) and diagonal, the furthest cell an alignment of cost \(s\) reaches, extended along matches at no cost, in \(O(ns)\) time in the worst case and \(O(n + s^2)\) expected time on random sequences \citep{Ukkonen1985,Myers1986ond}; WFA generalises it to gap-affine costs, where the wavefront, or front, of each cost has three layers \citep{MarcoSola2021wfa}, and BiWFA runs it from both ends \citep{MarcoSola2023biwfa}.

\subsection{The seed heuristic}

A*PA divides the reference into disjoint seeds of fixed length and finds their matches in the query, exactly or with one edit \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa}. The potential of a seed is the cost \(r\) of crossing it unmatched, 1 for exact seeds and 2 for seeds matched with one edit, and a match crosses a seed for less than \(r\). The gap-chaining seed heuristic charges a chain of matches from a cell the cost of each match and, for each gap between consecutive matches and from the last to the end, the larger of the potential of the seeds that start in the gap and the number of diagonals it shifts. Its value, the least charge of any chain, never exceeds the remaining cost, and A*PA keeps the match starts in layers by how much potential the best chain from each saves \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa}. A*PA2 prunes matches before the alignment, in place of A*PA's pruning during the search: a match \(\nu\) with cost \(c(\nu)\) and end cell \(\mathrm{end}(\nu)\) is kept only if a path from \(\mathrm{end}(\nu)\), starting at cost \(c(\nu)\), crosses the next \(p = 14\) seeds, counting that of \(\nu\), while its cost stays below the potential of the seeds it has crossed \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa2}. A diagonal transition from \(\mathrm{end}(\nu)\) tests this, dropping each furthest-reaching point whose cost reaches that potential; a further point on a diagonal has crossed at least as much potential, so no such path is missed. A*PA2 uses the heuristic to drop the rows of each band whose score plus the heuristic exceeds the bound \citep{GrootKoerkamp2024astarpa2}.
